ai-at-work.title: You don’t need to believe in a god to get a religious exemption from using AI at work
ai-at-work.excerpt: David Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, recently earned a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A University of Kentucky administrator successfully claimed a religious exemption from using AI at work, and apparently you don't actually need to belong to a recognized religion to qualify. This matters because it opens a potential loophole that HR teams will need to navigate carefully, turning what should be a straightforward policy conversation into something that now requires theological vetting. Look, I've been doing this for three decades, and when your exemption policy can't distinguish between genuine belief and a creative workaround, you've written a policy that's already dead on arrival.

ai-at-work.title: AWS will be a $1T business, Jassy says — but first, it will spend big
ai-at-work.excerpt: Amazon wants to be the king of AI cloud computing and become the first $1 trillion revenue business. But to do that it will have to continue on its capex spending spree, its CEO said Thursday.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AWS is betting massive infrastructure spending now will land them a $1 trillion revenue prize later, with AI as the primary growth engine. This matters because your cloud strategy and vendor relationships could shift dramatically if AWS wins the AI infrastructure race, potentially affecting everything from licensing costs to feature availability. Here's the thing though: every cloud provider is saying the same thing about AI dominance, so we'll see who actually executes versus who just talks a good game for Wall Street.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
ai-at-work.excerpt: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Thrive Holdings, which has OpenAI backing, is buying ADT for $15.3 billion and plans to inject AI into home security operations. This matters because it signals how AI investment money is flowing into unglamorous but essential services, and digital workplace leaders need to watch how AI transforms traditionally low-tech industries since those patterns will eventually hit your organization. Here's the thing: pouring billions into AI for home security is fine, but let's see if they actually make anyone's life better or just create another AI feature nobody asked for.

ai-at-work.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
ai-at-work.excerpt: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Mistral released the weights for a trillion-parameter AI model aimed at helping organizations build better cybersecurity defenses. This matters because digital workplace leaders are now facing a real choice between proprietary AI tools locked behind vendor gates and open models they can actually audit and customize for their own security needs. Honestly, after thirty years watching enterprises get trapped in vendor lock-in, watching an AI company hand over the keys feels less like innovation and more like someone finally admitting the emperor has no clothes.

tools-tech.title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
tools-tech.excerpt: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterp
tools-tech.dwp_take: Hackers are running a phishing scam that tricks employees into clicking fake Anthropic AI preview invites, then stealing their Google and Microsoft credentials. This matters because it shows employees are so desperate to play with the latest AI tools that they're bypassing basic security hygiene, which means your organization's access controls are only as strong as the person most excited about new tech. After thirty years watching workplace tech adoption, I can tell you that the fastest way to compromise enterprise security is to dangle something shiny in front of people who are already convinced they need it to stay relevant.

tools-tech.title: Apple brings touch to the Mac with $2,899 OLED MacBook Pro
tools-tech.excerpt: Following the release of the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro earlier this week, Apple has bought the “touch experience” to its professional laptop series, introducing a $2,899 (and up) MacBook Pro you can
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple added touch capability to the MacBook Pro lineup with their new M6 models starting at $2,899, complete with an OLED display and claimed 24-hour battery life. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because touch on laptops finally removes the friction between iPad workflows and desktop work, potentially changing how teams think about input methods and collaboration tools. Here's the thing though: we've been promised "touch laptops" before, and most professionals still prefer a trackpad for actual work, so let's see if this one actually sticks around or becomes another premium feature people don't use.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empo
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic and OpenAI just submitted competing proposals to California about who gets to kill dangerous AI models: Anthropic wants courts involved while OpenAI wants developers to hold the off switch. This matters because most enterprises deploying AI in their digital workplaces have zero clue who's actually responsible when things go sideways, and these regulatory frameworks will determine that accountability chain for years. Honestly, asking developers to police themselves on shutdown controls is like asking your teenager to set their own screen time limits, so I'm quietly rooting for the courts here.

digital-culture.title: Employee engagement in U.S. hits lowest point in 15 years
digital-culture.excerpt: Worker engagement in the U.S. has dropped below 30%, to its lowest level since 2011, Gallup reports. Engagement dropped two points from last quarter, equivalent to roughly 3.2 million fewer engaged wo
digital-culture.dwp_take: U.S. worker engagement just hit 30%, the worst in 15 years, with remote workers taking the hardest hit. This matters because your digital workplace strategy is directly connected to these numbers, and pretending it isn't won't change the fact that your tools, policies, and culture are now being measured against actual human motivation. Here's the thing: we built all this technology to make work better, yet engagement keeps dropping, which suggests we've been solving the wrong problems.

digital-culture.title: Instagram head Adam Mosseri warns creators that AI backlash is only going to get worse
digital-culture.excerpt: Instagram head Adam Mosseri said he expects anxiety and resentment about artificial intelligence to intensify over the next few years—and that social media platforms may be limited in their ability to
digital-culture.dwp_take: Adam Mosseri is essentially admitting that Instagram knows the AI backlash is coming and they can't really stop it. This matters because your employees are watching the same platforms you're pushing AI tools into, and they're absorbing this skepticism daily. Here's the thing: when leadership can't even control the narrative on their own platforms, maybe that's a signal to slow down your internal AI rollout and actually talk to people first instead of dropping it on them like a software update.

digital-culture.title: More companies like Microsoft are using buyouts. Should you take one?
digital-culture.excerpt: Microsoft is trying to cull its workforce by dangling an offer that might be hard for some employees to refuse. This week, the tech giant announced voluntary buyouts for 60,000 people, which is more t
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to over 60,000 employees, about 27 percent of its workforce, framing it as giving people agency over their futures. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals a major shift in how large tech companies are managing headcount, and you need to understand the real economics and timing before your leadership considers copying this playbook. Here's the thing: when a company with Microsoft's resources needs to shed a quarter of its people, calling it "voluntary agency" is like calling a layoff a "career pivot opportunity." Just read the fine print carefully.

digital-culture.title: 11 hybrid work rules that actually make sense
digital-culture.excerpt: Hybrid work succeeds when flexibility comes with clear expectations. Here, experts in the field share practical insights on how meetings, focus time, communication, and accountability can genuinely im
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company rounded up eleven practical hybrid work guidelines focused on flexibility paired with clear expectations around meetings, focus time, and accountability. This matters because most organizations are still fumbling the hybrid transition, and having actual evidence-based rules beats the usual corporate guessing game. My take: the fact that "trusting employees to decide their own attendance" is listed as a revolutionary rule tells you everything you need to know about how badly most companies have botched this whole thing.

industry-news.title: Discord Messages Are Coming to Web Search: Settings to Check
industry-news.excerpt: Discord messages from eligible public servers may appear in web search. Check rollout dates, privacy settings, and separate controls for AI summaries. The post Discord Messages Are Coming to Web Searc
industry-news.dwp_take: Discord is letting search engines index messages from public servers, meaning your late-night gaming rants might show up in Google results. This matters because digital workplace teams increasingly use Discord for collaboration, and suddenly your casual channel banter becomes permanently searchable and findable by anyone. Here's the thing: most people won't bother checking those privacy settings, so they'll accidentally turn their workplace Discord into a public record of every half-baked idea and complaint they've ever typed.

industry-news.title: Apple Touchscreen MacBook Pro Cheat Sheet: Price, Specs, and More
industry-news.excerpt: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro arrives Nov. 6. Explore pricing, M5 Pro and M5 Max specs, OLED features, battery life, and whether it's worth upgrading. The post Apple Touchscreen MacBook Pro Cheat Sh
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple is finally putting a touchscreen on the MacBook Pro starting November 6, complete with the new M5 Pro and M5 Max chips and an OLED display. For digital workplace folks, this matters because your Mac-loving employees will suddenly want these things, which means budget conversations and refresh cycle planning just got more interesting. Personally, I've watched Apple resist touchscreens on laptops for years while the rest of the industry moved on, so this feels less like innovation and more like they finally read the room.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Offers Buyouts to 60,000 Staff in Windows, Copilot
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, including Copilot and Windows staff. Here's what the workforce changes could mean for enterprise IT teams. The post Microsoft Offers Buyouts to
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees across Windows and Copilot divisions as part of workforce restructuring. This matters because when your primary productivity software vendor is actively shedding talent from core products, you should be paying attention to what that means for support, innovation cycles, and roadmap reliability. After three decades watching tech companies reshape themselves, I can tell you that "voluntary buyouts" is corporate speak for "we're making big bets and cleaning house," which usually creates a six to eighteen month window of organizational chaos before things stabilize, if they stabilize at all.

industry-news.title: Proton to Re-Interview Employees on AI Skills as Jobs Hang in Balance
industry-news.excerpt: Proton plans to reassess employees' AI skills in interviews that could affect their jobs, raising questions about AI adoption and workforce evaluations. The post Proton to Re-Interview Employees on AI
industry-news.dwp_take: Proton is conducting re-interviews to assess employee AI competency, with job security apparently tied to the results. This matters because it signals how organizations are weaponizing AI skills assessments as a hiring and retention tool, setting a precedent that could spread across tech and beyond. Here's my take: if your job security now hinges on proving you can use ChatGPT, we've officially jumped the shark on AI adoption theater, and someone in HR got way too excited about a shiny new evaluation metric.
